title: Chest pressure radiating to the arm and jaw in a regional emergency department
desc: This station involves a focused chest pain history and examination of a 64-year-old pizza shop manager brought by ambulance to a regional ED without a cardiac catheter laboratory. His pain returns during the history. The candidate then interprets his observations, 12-lead ECG, bloods and chest X-ray, recognises an anterior (anterolateral) STEMI, and outlines reperfusion when timely PCI is not available, along with immediate management and safety netting.
focus: Acute chest pain: a focused history, reading an anterior STEMI systematically, and choosing reperfusion in a regional hospital without PCI
stem:
You are the junior doctor in the Emergency Department of a regional hospital. The hospital has no cardiac catheter laboratory. Bradley (Brad) Oscar, a 64-year-old pizza shop manager, has been brought in by ambulance with chest pain. He is on a trolley in the acute area with an IV cannula, which the paramedics inserted, and he is on a cardiac monitor.

A nurse is with you and will carry out your instructions.
tasks: Take a focused history from Brad and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining. Act on anything the nurse tells you (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you Brad's observations, his 12-lead ECG, his blood results and his chest X-ray report. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Bradley (Brad) Oscar, a 64-year-old pizza shop manager, born 1 July 1957. The ambulance brought you in from work. You are lying propped up on the trolley, pale, cold and sweaty, holding your left arm. You are frightened but can talk in full sentences. A nurse is with the candidate and does what they ask. When the candidate says what they examine, the examiner gives the findings from the Exam findings below.

Opening line: "It's my chest, doc. It feels like a massive pressure, and my left arm feels like it's being squeezed."

History (give only when asked)

The pain

  • Site: the left side of your chest.
  • Onset: about 3 hours ago (around 11 am), while you were sitting doing the books at the shop. You were not lifting anything or exercising.
  • Character: a dull pain, "almost like an intense pressure".
  • Radiation: "It feels like my left arm is being squeezed, and my jaw feels a bit funny too."
  • Time course: constant since it came on, maybe getting a bit worse, until the ambulance treated it.
  • Relieving: "The ambos gave me something. It's good stuff, it's been less painful since then." If asked what: "a spray under my tongue and something through the drip". If asked about tablets: "No, I don't think they gave me any tablets."
  • Exacerbating (only if asked): you tried pressing on your chest and it did not make it worse. It does not change with moving, breathing or position.
  • Severity: 8/10 before the ambulance treatment, 4/10 now.
  • Previous episodes: you have never had chest pain or angina before.

Associated symptoms

  • Short of breath: yes, especially when the pain was at its worst. If asked: you do sometimes get short of breath after exercise.
  • Sweating: yes, you feel a bit cold and sweaty.
  • Nausea: yes, you have felt sick since yesterday. You have not vomited.
  • Bowels: you had to open your bowels right when the pain started; it was a bit loose, with no blood.
  • Say no if asked: no palpitations, no fainting or blackouts, no back pain, no tearing pain, no lying-flat breathlessness, no waking at night short of breath, no ankle swelling.

Other causes (all negative, give only if asked)

  • Lungs and clots: no cough, no fevers, no recent cold or sick contacts, no recent travel, no long trips or time off your feet, no calf pain or swelling. The pain is not worse when you breathe in.
  • Gut: no bloating. You rarely get heartburn; when you do, Gaviscon settles it, and it feels different from this pain.
  • Muscles and joints: no recent heavy lifting or exercise. The pain started at rest and is not worse with movement.

Past medical history

  • High blood pressure.
  • Gallbladder removed in 2014.
  • You do not see your GP very often; the last visit was about 5 years ago.
  • If asked about cholesterol: "Nobody's checked it in years." Diabetes: "Not that I know of."
  • If asked about your weight: about 92 kg.

Bleeding and medicine safety (only if asked)

  • No stroke, no bleeding problems, no stomach ulcers, no black stools or vomiting blood.
  • No recent operations, injuries or head knocks.
  • No blood thinners. No tablets for erections (such as Viagra).

Medications and allergies

  • Perindopril; you are not sure of the dose.
  • No over-the-counter medicines apart from occasional Gaviscon. No recreational drugs.
  • No known drug allergies.

Family history

  • Mother: died of breast cancer at 66.
  • Father: died of a heart attack at 61.
  • Brother and sister: both have high blood pressure and type 2 diabetes, but are alive and well.

Social history

  • Never smoked.
  • Alcohol: a couple of glasses of wine at dinner every night.
  • Exercise: "Not much anymore, my knees are painful."
  • Diet: "Could be healthier. My wife and I rely on takeaway a lot."
  • You manage a pizza shop. You live with your wife and are well supported by your workmates.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: "My heart is going to stop, don't let me die." "My poor wife will be left alone." You want them to fix it and to let your wife know where you are.

The nurse and how Brad changes

  • If asked for observations, the nurse gives the arrival set (14:05): HR 75, BP 152/90, RR 18, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C, BGL 7.4 mmol/L.
  • If asked about the ambulance handover: "The paramedics were with him from 13:35. They gave GTN 400 micrograms under the tongue twice and fentanyl 50 micrograms IV, and his pain went from 8 to 4. No aspirin is recorded on the sheet. Their 12-lead didn't transmit."
  • If asked for an ECG: "I recorded one at 14:10." The examiner says it will be given in Part 2.
  • If the candidate asks for bloods, a chest X-ray, monitoring, pads, a senior or a medicine, the nurse says, "Will do." The examiner notes it for marking in Part 2.
  • About 6 minutes into Part 1 (or when the examination starts, if sooner), the nurse says: "Doctor, his pain is back up to 6 out of 10 and I've seen a few early beats on the monitor." Brad says: "It's coming back, doc. It's getting tight again." His pulse is 84 and BP 148/88.
  • If the candidate reassesses him, gives GTN or analgesia, or explains what they are doing calmly, Brad settles a little but stays frightened.

Exam findings

  • General: anxious, pale, cool and clammy man, overweight, speaking in full sentences. No increased work of breathing. No xanthelasma.
  • Vital signs: as on the nurse's arrival set (after the nurse's report: HR 84, BP 148/88, pain 6/10).
  • Pulse: 84/min, irregular because of occasional early beats, normal volume. Radial pulses equal with no radio-radial delay; femoral pulses equal.
  • Blood pressure: right arm 152/90 mmHg, left arm 148/88 mmHg (taken one after the other).
  • Perfusion: cool, sweaty peripheries; CRT 2 seconds.
  • JVP: not raised.
  • Heart: apex not displaced. Dual heart sounds, no added sounds, no murmurs, no pericardial rub.
  • Chest: trachea central, equal expansion, resonant percussion, vesicular breath sounds, no crackles or wheeze.
  • Chest wall: not tender; pressing does not reproduce the pain.
  • Abdomen: soft and non-tender, including the epigastrium and right upper quadrant. Healed laparoscopic port scars. No pulsatile mass.
  • Legs: calves soft and non-tender, no swelling, no pitting oedema. Both knees show bony enlargement and crepitus.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self, confirms Brad's identity (name and date of birth) and explains what they are doing while he is in pain.

Recognises a possible acute coronary syndrome from the start. Straight away asks the nurse for the observations, continuous cardiac monitoring and the 12-lead ECG (within 10 minutes of arrival), and keeps the history focused.

Responds with empathy and in plain language to his fear of dying and his worry about his wife, without false reassurance. Can be earned in Part 1, or in Part 2 when Brad asks his question after question 3.
History
Characterises the chest pain:

kids.x: Site and character: left-sided, dull, like an intense pressure
Onset and time course: about 3 hours ago at rest, constant and getting a bit worse
Radiation: left arm squeezed, jaw feels funny
Severity 8/10 falling to 4/10 after ambulance treatment; not worse when pressing on the chest, moving or breathing

check.x: Asks about associated symptoms: breathlessness, sweating and nausea/vomiting, plus at least two of palpitations, syncope, orthopnoea/PND or ankle swelling.
Asks what the ambulance gave him and its effect, and establishes whether aspirin has been given (none recorded).
check.d: Credit asking Brad or the nurse.

check.x: Asks cluster questions for the other causes of chest pain:

kids.x: Aortic dissection: sudden tearing pain, pain going to the back
Pulmonary embolism or pneumothorax: pleuritic pain, travel or immobility, calf pain or swelling, cough, fever
Pericarditis or musculoskeletal: positional pain, recent viral illness, heavy lifting, pain on movement or chest wall pressure
Gastrointestinal: reflux (rare, settles with Gaviscon, feels different), bloating

check.x: Asks about previous chest pain or angina and exertional symptoms (none before; sometimes breathless after exercise).
Asks specifically about the major cardiac risk factors: hypertension (yes), cholesterol (not checked for years), type 2 diabetes (not known) and smoking (never).
check.d: Family history is credited in item 12.

check.x: Takes a family history: father died of a heart attack at 61, both siblings have hypertension and type 2 diabetes, mother died of breast cancer at 66.

Takes the past history, medications and allergies: hypertension, cholecystectomy in 2014, last GP visit 5 years ago; perindopril (dose unknown), no other prescription, OTC or recreational drugs; no known drug allergies.

Checks for contraindications to antithrombotic and fibrinolytic therapy (previous stroke, bleeding problems, peptic ulcer, recent surgery, trauma or head injury, anticoagulants) and asks about PDE5 inhibitors before GTN.
check.d: Credit the contraindication screen if it is done in Part 1 or stated before fibrinolysis in Part 2.

check.x: Takes a focused social history: alcohol (a couple of glasses of wine every night), exercise (limited by his knees), diet (takeaway), occupation, and who is at home (his wife).
Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations: believes his heart will stop and is worried his wife will be left alone.
Examination
Does a general inspection (pale, cool, clammy, anxious) and reviews the vital signs: HR, BP, RR, SpO2, temperature and BGL.
Compares the radial pulses and BP in both arms (and the femoral pulses), looking for the asymmetry of aortic dissection.
Examines the cardiovascular system: peripheral perfusion and CRT, JVP, heart sounds, a new murmur (mitral regurgitation, VSD), a third heart sound and a pericardial rub.
Examines the chest for crackles of pulmonary oedema and signs of pneumothorax, palpates the chest wall, and examines the abdomen and calves.

Responds to the nurse's report of returning pain and ectopics. Reassesses Brad at once and calls a senior. Also asks for at least two of: defibrillator pads, a repeat 12-lead ECG, or sublingual GTN or titrated IV analgesia after checking the BP.
Interpretation
Interprets the observations: all in the white zone, but returning pain, ectopics and nurse concern need immediate review.
Reads the ECG systematically:

kids.x: Confirms it is Brad's ECG recorded at 14:10
Normal axis, normal PR interval and narrow QRS

check.x: Identifies ST elevation in contiguous leads as a STEMI and states that the reperfusion decision rests on the ECG and symptoms, not on the troponin.

Localises it: ST elevation in V2 to V5 with I and aVL is an anterior STEMI with lateral extension (LAD territory), with reciprocal ST depression in III and Q waves in V2 to V4 showing established infarction.
Interprets the bloods: raised hs-troponin T and CK show myocardial injury; normal Hb, platelets, coagulation and renal function allow antithrombotics and fibrinolysis.
Interprets the chest X-ray: no pulmonary oedema, mediastinum not widened, no pneumothorax.

Gives anterior (anterolateral) STEMI as the most likely diagnosis and considers aortic dissection, with at least one feature against it (pressure not tearing, no back pain, equal arm BPs, normal mediastinum).
Gives other differentials, each with a feature against it: pulmonary embolism, pericarditis, and GORD or another GI cause.
Management
Gets the senior ED doctor to the bedside and phones the cardiologist at the nearest PCI-capable hospital at once to decide the reperfusion strategy.

States the reperfusion rule and applies it: primary PCI if first medical contact to device can be within 90 minutes; otherwise, with symptoms under 12 hours (3 hours here), fibrinolysis ideally within 30 minutes of arrival, then transfer to the PCI centre.

Before fibrinolysis, checks the contraindications (including suspected dissection and BP above 180/110) and gets consent. Names a fibrin-specific agent: tenecteplase (weight-based single bolus) or alteplase per local protocol.
Gives aspirin 300 mg chewed now (none given by ambulance), plus clopidogrel and an anticoagulant (enoxaparin or heparin) with fibrinolysis, or as the PCI cardiologist directs.
Treats the pain: sublingual GTN (SBP above 90, no PDE5 inhibitor) and small titrated IV opioid doses with an antiemetic. Gives oxygen only if SpO2 is below 93%, so none at 96%.
check.d: Accept an oxygen threshold of 90% or 94%, as long as routine oxygen is not given at 96%.

check.x: Monitors: continuous ECG with defibrillator pads, a repeat 12-lead ECG at 60 to 90 minutes after fibrinolysis, and rescue PCI if ST resolution is under 50% or pain or instability persists.
Arranges disposition and communication: retrieval or transfer to the PCI centre for angiography with CCU care. Explains the plan to Brad in plain words and offers to call his wife.
check.d: Credit from the management answer or the answer to Brad's question after question 3.

check.x: Safety netting

Tells Brad the warning signs in plain words, with a GTN action plan: stop, rest and use GTN for chest pain, and call 000 if it is severe, getting worse or lasts 10 minutes. Also report breathlessness, fainting, palpitations or bleeding.
Outlines secondary prevention: DAPT (aspirin plus P2Y12 inhibitor up to 12 months), high-intensity statin (LDL 4.1, untreated hypercholesterolaemia), beta blocker, continue perindopril, GTN spray.
Arranges follow-up: cardiac rehabilitation referral, GP review of risk factors (including HbA1c), and cardiology review with an echo.

part2.lead: Here are Brad's observations, the 12-lead ECG the nurse recorded at 14:10, his blood results and his portable chest X-ray report. The nearest PCI-capable hospital is about 3 hours by road; retrieval cannot get him to a cath lab within 90 minutes of first medical contact.
part2.patient:
Ask this straight after the examiner reads question 3. The candidate answers you as part of question 3.

  • "Am I going to die, doc? My wife will be on her own."

If the candidate explains clearly and honestly that this is a heart attack, that treatment to open the artery is starting and that they will call your wife, you settle and say thank you. If they use jargon ("STEMI", "thrombolysis", "PCI"), ask: "What does that mean?"

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Room air throughout. Before arrival the paramedics (with him from 13:35) gave GTN 400 micrograms sublingual twice and fentanyl 50 micrograms IV; pain fell from 8/10 to 4/10. No aspirin is recorded on the ambulance sheet. Monitor at 14:15: sinus rhythm with occasional early beats.
handover.model:
• Read: at 14:05 every value is in the white zone: RR 18, SpO2 96% on room air, BP 152/90, HR 75, temperature 36.6 °C, alert, BGL 7.4. At 14:15 the values are still white zone (HR 84, BP 148/88, SpO2 96%), but pain has risen from 4/10 to 6/10, there are new ectopic beats and the nurse is concerned.
  • Meaning: he is haemodynamically stable with no hypoxia and no signs of shock or heart failure. The returning pain is ongoing ischaemia, and ectopy in the first hours of a STEMI is a warning that dangerous arrhythmias (VF) are most likely in this period.
  • Changes: the zones alone do not trigger a call, but increasing pain and a worried nurse call for immediate medical review. With his ECG he needs a senior at the bedside now, continuous monitoring with pads on, and urgent reperfusion. No oxygen at 96%. BP is below 180/110, so it does not stop fibrinolysis, and it allows GTN.

rows.note: Arrived by ambulance; cardiac monitoring on
Pain back to 6/10; occasional early beats on monitor; doctor informed

handover.label: 12-lead ECG
handover.result:
12-lead ECG: Bradley Oscar, URN 1234567, DOB 01/07/1957. Recorded 02/07/2021 at 14:10 in the ED (25 mm/s, 10 mm/mV).

  • Rate: 75/min.
  • Rhythm: sinus rhythm, regular.
  • Axis: about +30° (normal).
  • P waves: normal morphology.
  • PR interval: 160 ms.
  • QRS: 96 ms. Q waves in V2, V3 and V4. No bundle branch block.
  • ST segments: ST elevation in V2 (3 mm), V3 (4 mm), V4 (3 mm) and V5 (2 mm), and in I (1.5 mm) and aVL (2 mm). ST depression of 1.5 mm in III. II, aVF, V1 and V6 show no significant ST change.
  • T waves: tall and broad in V2 to V4; inverted in III.
  • QTc: 430 ms (Bazett).
  • U waves: none.
  • Comparison: no previous ECG on file.
handover.model:
• Read: confirms it is Brad's ECG recorded at 14:10. Sinus rhythm at 75/min, normal axis, normal PR interval. Narrow QRS with Q waves in V2 to V4. ST elevation in V2 to V5 (2 to 4 mm) and in I and aVL, with reciprocal ST depression in III. QTc normal, no old ECG.
  • Meaning: ST elevation in contiguous leads, above the threshold for a man over 40 (2 mm in V2 to V3, 1 mm elsewhere), with 3 hours of ischaemic pain: an anterior STEMI with lateral extension (anterolateral), from occlusion of the left anterior descending artery. The involvement of I and aVL suggests a proximal occlusion. The Q waves show the infarct is already established, but he is well within the 12-hour window. The ectopic beats seen on the monitor at 14:15 matter because VF is most likely in the first hours of a STEMI.
  • Changes: activate reperfusion now on the ECG, with no wait for the troponin. Put defibrillator pads on and repeat the ECG with any change in pain, and at 60 to 90 minutes after fibrinolysis to look for ST resolution.

handover.label: Bloods
handover.result: Collected 14:20 from a new IV cannula, about 3 hours 20 minutes after pain onset. Lipids non-fasting.
handover.model:
• Read: hs-troponin T 186 ng/L, more than 10 times the 99th percentile, and CK 620 U/L: acute myocardial injury. AST 64 is mildly raised (also released from injured myocardium) with a normal ALT. Hb 148, platelets 245, INR 1.0 and APTT 29 are normal. Potassium 4.2, magnesium 0.84 and creatinine 78 are normal. Random glucose 7.6 is within range. Total cholesterol 6.2, LDL 4.1 and triglycerides 2.4 are high, HDL 0.9 is low.
  • Meaning: the troponin fits the STEMI but did not decide it; the ECG did. Nothing in the bloods stops aspirin, clopidogrel, enoxaparin or fibrinolysis, and the normal renal function allows standard enoxaparin dosing. Normal potassium and magnesium lower the arrhythmia risk. The lipids show untreated hypercholesterolaemia.
  • Changes: do not wait for a repeat troponin before reperfusion. Start a high-intensity statin. With his family history, check HbA1c once he is stable.

rows.n: about 3 h 20 min after pain onset

handover.label: Portable chest X-ray
handover.result:
Examination: chest X-ray, portable AP semi-erect, 14:30.

Clinical details: 64-year-old man with 3 hours of left-sided chest pain and ST elevation on ECG. ?Pulmonary oedema ?Mediastinal widening.

Findings:

  • Lines and devices: ECG electrodes over the chest.
  • Lungs: clear. No consolidation. No upper lobe venous diversion, no interstitial or alveolar oedema, no Kerley B lines.
  • Pleura: no pleural effusion. No pneumothorax.
  • Heart and mediastinum: heart size within normal limits for an AP film. Mediastinum not widened; aortic knuckle normal in contour. Trachea central.
  • Upper abdomen: surgical clips in the right upper quadrant, consistent with previous cholecystectomy. No free subdiaphragmatic gas.
  • Bones and soft tissues: no acute bony abnormality.

Conclusion: no acute cardiopulmonary abnormality. No pulmonary oedema, no mediastinal widening and no pneumothorax.
handover.model:
• Read: an adequate portable AP film with clear lungs, no oedema or effusions, no pneumothorax, normal heart size for an AP film, a mediastinum that is not widened, a normal aortic knuckle, and cholecystectomy clips.
  • Meaning: no heart failure (Killip class I, which fits the clear chest). A normal mediastinum makes aortic dissection less likely, but it does not exclude it; the clinical picture (no tearing or back pain, equal arm BPs) matters more. No pneumothorax or pneumonia.
  • Changes: nothing here stops fibrinolysis. The X-ray must never delay reperfusion; it is done while the reperfusion decision is being made.

ask: You are now calling the on-call cardiologist at the nearest PCI-capable hospital. Please give an ISBAR handover of Brad, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Brad now, here in this regional emergency department.
Before Brad goes home after his treatment, what would you tell him and what follow-up would you arrange?
expect:
• Identify: self, ED doctor at the regional hospital; Bradley Oscar, 64.
  • Situation: anterior (anterolateral) STEMI, pain onset about 3 hours ago, pain returning; haemodynamically stable.
  • Background: left-sided pressure to left arm and jaw with sweating, nausea and breathlessness. Hypertension on perindopril, father MI at 61. Ambulance gave GTN and fentanyl, no aspirin. No bleeding, stroke or anticoagulant contraindications.
  • Assessment: obs white zone (HR 84, BP 148/88, SpO2 96% RA) but pain returning with ectopics. ECG: sinus 75, ST elevation V2 to V5, I, aVL, reciprocal III, Q waves V2 to V4: proximal LAD; activating reperfusion on the ECG, not waiting for troponin. Troponin 186, CK 620: myocardial injury. Hb, platelets, coagulation, renal function normal. CXR: no oedema, normal mediastinum, no pneumothorax.
  • Recommendation: PCI not possible within 90 minutes, so agree fibrinolysis now, then transfer; advise on antithrombotics.

Anterior (anterolateral) STEMI from LAD occlusion: 3 hours of pressure-like pain to the arm and jaw, sweating, nausea and breathlessness, hypertension and family history, ST elevation V2 to V5, I and aVL with reciprocal III, raised troponin.

  • Aortic dissection (must exclude before fibrinolysis): against: no tearing or back pain, equal arm BPs, normal mediastinum.
  • Pulmonary embolism: against: not pleuritic, no risk factors, SpO2 96%, normal calves.
  • Pericarditis: against: not positional, no rub, territorial ST elevation with reciprocal change and Q waves.
  • GORD or oesophageal pain: against: heartburn is rare, settles with Gaviscon and feels different; the ECG.

1. Senior ED doctor now; monitoring, defibrillator pads, second cannula.
  2. Phone the PCI-centre cardiologist: PCI not achievable within 90 minutes (3 hours away), so fibrinolysis within 30 minutes of arrival.
  3. Check contraindications, consent; tenecteplase weight-based bolus (50 mg at 92 kg) or alteplase.
  4. Aspirin 300 mg chewed now; clopidogrel 300 mg; enoxaparin 30 mg IV, then 1 mg/kg SC 12-hourly, first SC dose 15 minutes after the IV bolus; maximum 100 mg for each of the first two SC doses (92 mg for Brad); or heparin.
  5. GTN, titrated IV opioid with antiemetic; no oxygen at 96%.
  6. Repeat ECG at 60 to 90 minutes: under 50% ST resolution or ongoing pain means rescue PCI; transfer regardless.
  7. When Brad asks: answers honestly in plain words (a heart attack, treatment to open the artery is starting, most people recover well); offers to call his wife.

• Red flags: chest pain: stop, rest, use GTN; call 000 if severe, worsening or lasting 10 minutes. Also breathlessness, fainting, palpitations, bleeding.
  • Medicines: DAPT (aspirin plus P2Y12 inhibitor up to 12 months), high-intensity statin, beta blocker, continue perindopril, GTN spray.
  • Follow-up: cardiac rehabilitation referral; GP review of risk factors (including HbA1c); cardiology review with an echo.

ddx.dx: Anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction with lateral extension (left anterior descending artery occlusion)
ddx.for: Three hours of left-sided pressure to the left arm and jaw with sweating, nausea and breathlessness, hypertension and a father with an MI at 61, ST elevation in V2 to V5, I and aVL with reciprocal depression in III, and a raised troponin.
He has hypertension and severe chest pain, and dissection must be excluded before fibrinolysis.
ddx.against: The pain is a gradual pressure, not tearing, with no back pain, his arm BPs and pulses are equal, and the mediastinum is not widened.

ddx.for: He has chest pain with breathlessness.
ddx.against: The pain is not pleuritic, he has no travel, immobility or calf symptoms, SpO2 is 96% on room air, and the ECG shows territorial ST elevation.

ddx.for: He has chest pain with ST elevation.
ddx.against: No viral illness, the pain is not positional or pleuritic, there is no rub, and the ST elevation is territorial with reciprocal depression and Q waves.

ddx.for: He has occasional heartburn and nausea.
ddx.against: His heartburn is rare, settles with Gaviscon and feels different, and the pain goes to the arm and jaw with sweating and a STEMI on the ECG.

guide:
In Part 1, Brad answers the history and the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings when the candidate says what they examine. The nurse gives the arrival observations and the ambulance handover when asked. About 6 minutes in, or as the examination begins, the nurse reports the returning pain and ectopics; mark the bedside response (item 22) in Part 1. If the candidate asks for the ECG, the nurse says it was recorded at 14:10 and the examiner will give it in Part 2. This is an artefact of the format: in practice it would be read within 10 minutes of arrival. Note any treatment ordered in Part 1 (aspirin, GTN, analgesia, pads, calling the cardiologist) and credit it against the Management items in Part 2.

In Part 2, read the lead (including the distance to the PCI centre), hand over all four results, then ask the four questions in order. Credit item 34 if the candidate states the rule (PCI within 90 minutes of first medical contact, otherwise fibrinolysis) and applies it to Brad. Accept tenecteplase or alteplase. Accept 'anterior' or 'anterolateral' STEMI for item 27. Accept an oxygen threshold of 90%, 93% or 94%, as long as the candidate does not give routine oxygen at 96%. Brad's question comes straight after question 3 is read; credit items 4 and 39 from the answer (item 4 if it was not earned in Part 1).

A high-performing candidate asks for monitoring and the ECG in the first minute and takes a SOCRATES history of the pain with its associated symptoms. They find out what the ambulance gave and notice that no aspirin was given. They screen for dissection, PE, pericarditis and GI causes, take the risk factors and family history, and check the bleeding and stroke history. They act at once when the pain returns. In Part 2 they read the ECG systematically from patient details to ST segments, call it an anterior STEMI with lateral extension from the LAD, and do not wait for the troponin. They recognise that timely PCI is not available and choose fibrinolysis with aspirin, clopidogrel and enoxaparin, then transfer. They plan a repeat ECG to look for reperfusion, and safety-net in plain words with a GTN action plan and cardiac rehabilitation.

A borderline candidate takes a long, unfocused history and does not ask about ambulance treatment or bleeding risk. They call the ECG "ST changes" without a territory, wait for the troponin, or ask for "cardiology review" without a reperfusion decision. They may plan transfer for PCI without considering the time, or give fibrinolysis without checking contraindications.

Allow about 75–90 seconds for each question, keeping Part 2 within 5 minutes.
explain:
Diagnosis: anterior STEMI with lateral extension

Brad has 3 hours of left-sided, pressure-like chest pain radiating to the left arm and jaw, with sweating, nausea and breathlessness. He has hypertension, a sedentary lifestyle, a poor diet, untreated hypercholesterolaemia and a father who died of a heart attack. His ECG shows ST elevation in V2 to V5, I and aVL with reciprocal depression in III. That is an anterior STEMI extending laterally (anterolateral), from occlusion of the left anterior descending artery; involvement of I and aVL suggests a proximal lesion. STEMI is a clinical and ECG diagnosis. Reperfusion does not wait for the troponin.

A type 1 myocardial infarction follows rupture of an atherosclerotic plaque. Platelets aggregate and a thrombus forms on the plaque. A completely occlusive thrombus causes a full-thickness infarct (STEMI); a partly occlusive one causes NSTEMI or unstable angina.

The focused history

Characterise the pain (site, onset, character, radiation, associated symptoms, time course, exacerbating and relieving factors, severity). Then ask cluster questions for the dangerous mimics: aortic dissection (tearing pain to the back), PE and pneumothorax (pleuritic pain, immobility, calf symptoms), pericarditis (positional pain, viral prodrome), and GI and musculoskeletal causes. Ask specifically about hypertension, cholesterol, diabetes, smoking and family history. Always ask what the ambulance gave, because the next doses depend on it. Before antithrombotics and fibrinolysis, ask about stroke, bleeding, ulcers, recent surgery or trauma and anticoagulants; before GTN, ask about PDE5 inhibitors. Women, older people and people with diabetes more often present atypically, with epigastric, jaw, arm or back pain, or breathlessness without pain.

Interpreting the ECG

When time is short, state the key finding first ("ST elevation in V2 to V5, I and aVL: anterolateral STEMI"), then go through the ECG systematically:

  1. Patient details and the date and time of the ECG; calibration (10 mm/mV, two large squares) and paper speed
  2. Heart rate and rhythm
  3. Cardiac axis
  4. P waves
  5. PR interval
  6. QRS complex
  7. ST segments
  8. T waves
  9. U waves
  10. Comparison with previous ECGs and documentation

STEMI criteria are new ST elevation at the J point in two or more contiguous leads: in V2 to V3 at least 2 mm in men aged 40 or over (2.5 mm under 40) and 1.5 mm in women, and at least 1 mm in other leads. Brad's ECG also shows Q waves in V2 to V4, showing infarction is already established. His rhythm, axis, PR interval and QRS width are otherwise normal. The ectopic beats seen later on the monitor are not dangerous in themselves, but VF is most likely in the first hours of a STEMI, so continuous monitoring with defibrillator pads on is essential. Repeat the ECG every 15 to 30 minutes while pain continues, and with any change.

Reperfusion in a regional hospital

The Australian ACS guideline recommends reperfusion for STEMI presenting within 12 hours of symptom onset. Primary PCI is preferred if it can be delivered within 90 minutes of first medical contact. Where it cannot, as in a regional hospital 3 hours from a cath lab, fibrinolysis is given, ideally within 30 minutes of arrival, after checking contraindications. A fibrin-specific agent is used: tenecteplase as a weight-based single bolus or alteplase as an infusion, per local protocol. The patient is then transferred to a PCI-capable hospital (a pharmaco-invasive strategy). Rescue PCI is needed if ST elevation has not resolved by at least 50% at 60 to 90 minutes, or if pain or instability persist. Speak to the PCI centre early, because they help decide which path to take.

Absolute contraindications to fibrinolysis include previous intracranial haemorrhage, ischaemic stroke within 3 months, a known cerebral vascular lesion or intracranial tumour, suspected aortic dissection, active bleeding, and significant head or facial trauma within 3 months. Relative contraindications include uncontrolled hypertension (above 180/110), recent major surgery or internal bleeding, non-compressible vascular punctures, active peptic ulcer, pregnancy and oral anticoagulation. Brad has none.

Immediate management

  • DRSABCD, call for senior help, continuous monitoring, defibrillator pads and IV access.
  • Oxygen only if hypoxic; the Australian guideline advises against routine oxygen when SpO2 is 93% or above.
  • Aspirin 300 mg chewed if not already given by the ambulance, as here.
  • With fibrinolysis: clopidogrel (300 mg loading dose at 75 years or under) and an anticoagulant, such as enoxaparin 30 mg IV then 1 mg/kg subcutaneously 12-hourly in patients under 75 (first SC dose 15 minutes after the IV bolus; maximum 100 mg for each of the first two SC doses, 92 mg for Brad), or unfractionated heparin. With primary PCI, the P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor or prasugrel preferred) and anticoagulant follow the interventional cardiologist.
  • Sublingual GTN for ischaemic pain if SBP is above 90 and no PDE5 inhibitor has been taken; titrated IV opioid with an antiemetic.
  • Bloods (troponin, FBC, UEC, LFT, CK, coagulation, lipids, glucose) and a chest X-ray, without delaying reperfusion.

Complications to watch for

Within 24 hours: sudden cardiac death, arrhythmias, acute left heart failure and cardiogenic shock. At 1 to 3 days: pericarditis. At 3 to 14 days: mechanical complications (papillary muscle rupture with mitral regurgitation, septal rupture, free wall rupture with tamponade). After 2 weeks: ventricular aneurysm, mural thrombus with embolism, Dressler syndrome, heart failure and reinfarction. A large anterior infarct carries a higher risk of LV dysfunction and mural thrombus, which is why an echo matters.

Secondary prevention and follow-up

Following the Australian ACS guideline and the ACSQHC Acute Coronary Syndromes Clinical Care Standard, Brad needs:

  • aspirin long term with a P2Y12 inhibitor for up to 12 months
  • a high-intensity statin (LDL 4.1 untreated)
  • a beta blocker
  • continued ACE inhibitor (he already takes perindopril)
  • a GTN spray with a written action plan
  • referral to cardiac rehabilitation before discharge.

Lifestyle advice covers a healthier diet with less takeaway, activity that suits his knees, and alcohol within the NHMRC guideline (no more than 10 standard drinks a week); a couple of glasses of wine every night is above this. He has not seen a GP for 5 years and both siblings have type 2 diabetes, so his GP should check HbA1c and manage his risk factors. Under Austroads, private drivers do not drive for 2 weeks after an MI.

Safety netting

For chest pain he should stop, rest and use his GTN, and call 000 if the pain is severe, getting worse or lasts 10 minutes. He should also seek help urgently for breathlessness, fainting, palpitations or bleeding on dual antiplatelet therapy. Acknowledge his fear honestly and involve his wife.
points: STEMI is an ECG and clinical diagnosis: ST elevation in two or more contiguous leads (in V2 to V3 at least 2 mm in men 40 or over, 1 mm in other leads) with ischaemic symptoms. Reperfusion never waits for the troponin.

Read every ECG systematically, from patient details and calibration through rate, rhythm, axis, PR, QRS, ST and T waves, but state the key finding first. ST elevation in V2 to V5 with I and aVL and reciprocal III is an anterolateral STEMI from the LAD.

Primary PCI is preferred if it can be done within 90 minutes of first medical contact. In a regional hospital where it cannot, give fibrinolysis within 30 minutes of arrival (symptoms under 12 hours), then transfer for angiography.

Before fibrinolysis, screen for contraindications, including stroke, bleeding, recent surgery or head injury, suspected aortic dissection and BP above 180/110. Give aspirin 300 mg, clopidogrel and enoxaparin or heparin alongside it.
Always ask what the ambulance gave. Give aspirin if it was not given, GTN for ongoing pain if SBP is above 90 with no PDE5 inhibitor, and oxygen only if SpO2 is below 93%.
After STEMI: dual antiplatelet therapy for up to 12 months, a high-intensity statin, a beta blocker, an ACE inhibitor, a GTN action plan, cardiac rehabilitation and GP follow-up of risk factors.
